q: Wreck, bystanders still in the roadway. Crew, bystanders, and the patient are already on your safety list. Which leftover person sits first?

opts.t: You first, then crew, then bystanders, then the patient
opts.why: Safety order: you, crew, bystanders, patient.

opts.t: Crew first, then you, then bystanders, then the patient
opts.why: You sit first, not crew.

opts.t: Patient first, then crew, then bystanders, then you
opts.why: Patient is last.

opts.t: MOI is crash force plus hidden injury; NOI is always both at once
opts.why: Testing is a clean split.

opts.why: Stay out.

opts.t: Walk in and treat it as eight separate asthma attacks

q: More than one patient shows up in this course block. Docs and abandonment still matter. Which leftover rule is true now versus later MCI?

opts.why: This course block = one patient. MCI later flips the first five weeks.

opts.why: This block is one-patient.

opts.why: MCI later flips those early rules.

opts.why: This block is still one-patient.

q: A stem does not name your partner's level. You will still request extra help if needed. Which leftover assumption is true?

opts.t: EMT on an ambulance; request medics unless the stem names a medic

q: Medical and trauma skill sheets share six scene lines. Safety, MOI/NOI, count, extra help, and consider C-spine are already in the set. Which leftover first step and order is right?

opts.t: BSI then safety then MOI/NOI then count then extra help then consider C-spine
opts.why: Six lines: BSI, safety, MOI/NOI, number of patients, extra resources, consider C-spine.

opts.t: Safety then BSI then extra help then C-spine then count then MOI/NOI
opts.why: BSI is first; C-spine is last of the six.

opts.t: BSI then safety then extra help then count then MOI/NOI then skip C-spine
opts.why: MOI/NOI comes before count; C-spine stays.

opts.t: MOI/NOI then BSI then safety then count then extra help then consider C-spine
opts.why: BSI and safety come first.

q: Primary, history, secondary, and reassess are already on the run. Which leftover first bucket completes the five-part test split?

opts.t: Scene, then primary, then history, then secondary, then reassess
opts.why: Five pieces: scene, primary, history, secondary, reassess.

opts.t: Primary, then scene, then history, then secondary, then reassess
opts.why: Scene is first.

opts.why: Primary comes before history and secondary.

q: The primary-assessment slice is the biggest NREMT bucket. 10 to 15 percent and 70 to 80 percent are already off. Which leftover size is listed?

opts.t: About 35 to 45 percent, the biggest slice
opts.why: Primary is about 35 to 45 percent of the test.

opts.t: About 10 to 15 percent, the smallest slice
opts.why: That is too small.

opts.t: About 70 to 80 percent, the only slice
opts.why: That is too large.

opts.t: About 35 to 45 percent, the smallest slice
opts.why: It is the biggest slice, not the smallest.

q: You get eyes on a still, blue, unresponsive person. A&O questions and history are later. Which leftover first GI question is true?

opts.t: Could they be dead? If maybe, check a pulse and start CPR now
opts.why: First GI question: could they be dead? If maybe, pulse and CPR now.

opts.t: Could they be dead? If maybe, finish A&O x4 then start CPR
opts.why: Do not finish A&O first.

opts.t: Could they be hungry? If maybe, check a pulse and start CPR now
opts.why: The question is death, not hunger.

opts.t: Could they be dead? If maybe, skip the pulse and start history
opts.why: Check a pulse.

q: Mute on the couch, looking around, family says this is new. A calm GI can sit on a time-sensitive brain problem. Which leftover statement is true?

opts.t: Calm GI can be wrong; a time-sensitive brain problem can still sit there
opts.why: GI can be wrong (mute stroke; out was asleep). Looks-fine stroke is still time-sensitive — get going.

opts.t: Calm GI proves they are fine; a mute stroke is off the list
opts.why: Mute stroke is the trap.

opts.t: Calm GI can be wrong; only a trauma problem can still sit there
opts.why: Stroke is the example.

opts.t: Calm GI proves they are fine; stay put until speech comes back
opts.why: Get going.

q: Bright-red spurting from an arm as you walk up. Airway and later boxes are still on the sheet. Which leftover move is now?

opts.t: Treat the bleed now; a life threat does not wait for its later box
opts.why: Find a life threat, treat that life threat. Bright-red spurting: treat now.

opts.t: Save the bleed for circulation on the sheet; finish airway first
opts.why: Treat the life threat now.

opts.t: Treat the bleed now; only after you finish the full secondary
opts.why: Do not wait for the secondary.

opts.t: Save the bleed for history; a life threat waits for its later box
opts.why: It does not wait.

q: Slumped on the couch, eyes shut, no look when you walk in. Sitting up on furniture is already a trap. Which leftover AVPU letter is true?

opts.t: Not A; sitting up does not make them awake and looking
opts.why: A = awake/alert, looking around. Slumped couch is not awake.

opts.t: A, because they are sitting up on furniture
opts.why: Sitting is not A.

opts.t: U already; you skip voice and pain entirely
opts.why: You still check voice then pain.

opts.t: V already; slumped means they answered your name
opts.why: They have not answered.

q: You say your name. They mutter hey or the eyes flicker. A sternal rub is already unnecessary if you have a level. Which leftover next move is true?

opts.t: Call them V and stop; do not add a pain check
opts.why: V = any response to voice. Stop when you get a level. No pain if already A or V.

opts.t: Call them A and stop; do not add a pain check
opts.why: A is awake and looking around.

opts.t: Call them V and keep going; add a sternal rub anyway
opts.why: Do not add pain if already V.

opts.t: Call them U and stop; a mutter does not count as voice
opts.why: A mutter counts as voice.

q: No response to voice. Sternal knuckles, trap pinch, and nail squeeze are already on the pain list. They moan, swat, or turn away. What AVPU letter is that?

opts.t: P
opts.why: P = those pain checks. Any moan, swat, or turn-away = pain.

opts.t: A, because only a full sentence counts
opts.why: A sentence is more than required.

opts.t: V, because a light tap on the hair or a wave only is enough
opts.why: Those are not the listed pain checks.

opts.t: U, because a pain check only counts after they already answer to your voice
opts.why: If they already answer to voice they are V; you stop.

q: No response to a real pain check. A&O x4 is already off. Which leftover AVPU letter is left?

opts.t: Call them U and stop; there are no further LOC checks
opts.why: U = no response to pain. No further checks.

opts.t: Keep going to A&O x4 because U still has more checks
opts.why: U has no further LOC checks.

opts.t: Call them P and stop; no response still means pain
opts.why: No response is U, not P.

opts.t: Call them V and stop; pain failure upgrades them to voice
opts.why: Pain failure does not upgrade them.

q: Awake, misses the year, no good excuse. Expressed consent is already off unless a miss is reasonable. Which leftover consent path is true?

opts.t: Implied, unless a circumstantial miss makes that miss reasonable
opts.why: Miss one means implied consent unless circumstantial. Unsure: treat or medical control.

opts.why: One miss does not prove full capacity.

opts.why: A circumstantial miss can keep it from being implied.

opts.t: Expressed, unless they also miss their own name on the same pass
opts.why: Any one miss can flip it.

q: They nail name, place, year, and president. Always/never/guarantee words are already traps. Which leftover capacity statement is true?

opts.why: Guarantee is a trap.

opts.t: No case at all; x4 is only used for infants on this sheet
opts.why: x4 is for this awake adult.

opts.t: Strong case, and a guarantee; always/never words are required
opts.why: Not a guarantee.

opts.t: Onset is when it started; timing is what you were doing
opts.why: Those are swapped.

opts.t: Onset is the 0 to 10 number; timing is what you were doing
opts.why: 0 to 10 is severity.

opts.t: Onset is what you were doing; timing is the 0 to 10 number
opts.why: Timing is when it started.

q: Pain word. Planting left arm and a single leading label are already banned. Which leftover quality ask is listed?

opts.t: Let them pick a word; do not plant left arm or a single leading label
opts.why: No leading questions. Their word. Too many options if they stall. Do not ask if it radiates down the left arm.

opts.t: Plant left arm first; then force a single leading label
opts.why: Do not plant left-arm radiation.

opts.t: Let them pick a word; then plant left arm before they answer where
opts.why: Do not plant left arm.

opts.t: Skip quality; SAMPLE already covers the pain word
opts.why: Q is OPQRST. SAMPLE is the broader PMH set.

q: Nobody knows the unresponsive park patient. No family, jewelry, wallet, or phone data. Inventing SAMPLE is already off. Which leftover history next is true?

opts.t: Empty history is allowed; move to the secondary exam
opts.why: No data means history is out the window, then secondary.

opts.t: Empty history is not allowed; invent SAMPLE before you move
opts.why: You can have nothing and still move.

opts.t: Empty history is allowed; move back to scene size-up only
opts.why: Next is secondary.

opts.t: Empty history is not allowed; strip them for a home medical scan
opts.why: Unresponsive park is not a home chest-pain strip.

q: They deny drugs. You still think they used. EMT meds are not directly impacted. Which leftover second-ask move is listed?

opts.t: Ask once more with no judgment; second deny, drop it and chart they deny
opts.why: You may ask a second time, no judgment, not the cops. Deny again: drop it. Chart patient denies.

opts.t: Ask once more with no judgment; second deny, keep pressing until they confess
opts.why: Second deny: drop it.

opts.t: Skip the second ask; EMT meds change if they have alcohol
opts.why: EMT meds are not directly impacted. You may ask twice.

opts.t: Call them a liar in the PCR so law enforcement has a quote
opts.why: Chart denies or what they state.

q: You suspect abuse. Walking the hallway naming them an abuser is already defamation. Which leftover report rule is true?

opts.t: Report the suspicion and what you saw; that is not defamation if later false
opts.why: Mandatory report of suspicion. Not defamation if untrue. Public accusation is defamation.

opts.t: Stay quiet; a false suspicion is automatically defamation
opts.why: Reporting a suspicion is not a defamation problem.

opts.t: Walk the hallway saying they are a child abuser so staff hears
opts.why: That public accusation is defamation.

opts.t: Write in the PCR who did it and skip law enforcement
opts.why: Objective observations plus quoted statements. Get LE if needed. Do not accuse.

q: Childbearing-age woman, lower belly pain. Any abdominal pain also gets N/V/D and bowel/bladder. Headache is already the STD counter-example. Which leftover Sunday questions are listed?

opts.t: Any chance you are pregnant, and when was your last period
opts.why: Consider all childbearing-age females with lower abdominal pain possibly pregnant. Ask pregnancy chance plus LMP.

opts.t: Skip pregnancy; only ask if dispatch said OB
opts.why: Consider them possibly pregnant on that complaint.

opts.t: Any chance you are pregnant, and skip bowel and bladder on all belly pain
opts.why: Any abdominal pain also gets bowel/bladder.

opts.t: Ask STD questions on every headache so you do not miss one
opts.why: STDs only if the call fits. Headache is the counter-example.

q: Awake, medical chest pain. They can point to the part. Ejected wreck is already the detailed example. Which leftover exam is true?

opts.t: Focused on the chest; a talking medical can point to the part
opts.why: Focused if you know the part — conscious medical. Detailed if unconscious or significant MOI.

opts.t: Detailed head-to-toe; every medical gets a full strip
opts.why: Talking medical chest pain: focus the chest.

opts.t: Focused on the chest; also used for the ejected wreck with arm pain
opts.why: Ejected / significant MOI = detailed even if they are awake.

opts.t: Skip the exam; vitals already happened in the primary
opts.why: Full vitals and the physical sit in the secondary.

q: Stepped-on-leg snap, no fall, versus ejected and talking. Rapid scan is already the primary trauma sweep. Which leftover secondary exam pair is true?

opts.t: Isolated step = focused leg; ejected = full detailed even if they talk
opts.why: Low-MOI isolated complaint can focus. Significant MOI (ejected) = head-to-toe.

opts.t: Isolated step = full detailed; ejected = focused arm only
opts.why: Opposite.

opts.t: Both get a 60-second primary rapid scan only and no secondary
opts.why: This is the secondary focused vs detailed choice.

opts.t: Both skip exam if they can still talk
opts.why: Talking only lets you focus when the MOI is isolated.

q: Joint deformity: assume broken. Cyanosis, AVPU, pulse, SAMPLE, and vitals are already the wrong letters. Deformity, contusions, abrasions, punctures, burns, tenderness, lacerations, and swelling are already the eight signs. What named set is that?

opts.t: DCAP-BTLS
opts.why: DCAP-BTLS = those eight injury signs.

opts.t: A primary/history mix of deformity, cyanosis, AVPU, pulse, burns, tenderness, lacerations, SAMPLE
opts.why: Those mix primary/history letters.

opts.t: A vital mix of deformity, contusions, airway, pupils, blood pressure, GCS, lungs, sugar
opts.why: Vitals are not DCAP-BTLS.

opts.t: Lacerations and swelling only, with the rest waiting for X-ray
opts.why: All eight are listed.

q: Snore, gurgle, and stridor are heard standing in front of you. EMTs still auscultate. Which leftover trio is lower-airway (scope on the chest)?

opts.t: Wheeze, crackles, rhonchi
opts.why: Upper heard in front of you. Lower need a stethoscope on the chest.

opts.t: Snore, gurgle, stridor as the lower set
opts.why: Those three are upper.

opts.t: All six are upper; EMTs do not auscultate
opts.why: EMTs still auscultate.

opts.t: Crackles are upper tongue; snore is pulmonary edema
opts.why: Snore = tongue. Crackles = fluid in the lower airway / pulmonary edema.

q: Snore is tongue. Asthma wheeze is high-pitched mostly on exhalation. Stridor is upper. Which leftover crackles versus rhonchi pair is listed?

opts.t: Crackles = fluid / pulmonary edema (straw bubbles); rhonchi = mucus / pneumonia (low rattle)
opts.why: Crackles = edema or drown fluid. Rhonchi = junky mucus, classic pneumonia. EMT does not treat the infection.

opts.t: Crackles = mucus / pneumonia; rhonchi = tongue in the throat
opts.why: Tongue is snoring. Pneumonia was the rhonchi example.

opts.t: Crackles = high-pitched exhalation asthma; rhonchi = upper stridor
opts.why: Those are wheeze and stridor.

opts.t: Both are upper sounds you hear without a stethoscope
opts.why: Both are lower-airway, stethoscope sounds.

q: First blood pressure is by hand, then machines if they still make sense. Cuff about two-thirds of the upper arm. Too small reads falsely high. Which leftover first-BP and too-big pair is listed?

opts.t: First one manual; a cuff that is too big reads falsely low
opts.why: First BP by hand. Too big: falsely low; too small: falsely high.

opts.t: First one machine-only; a cuff that is too big reads falsely high
opts.why: First is manual. Too big is falsely low.

opts.t: First one manual; a cuff that is too big reads falsely high
opts.why: Too big is falsely low.

opts.t: Skip BP under age ten because 90 is only for adults
opts.why: Under ten use (2 x age) + 70. Under three is usually no cuff small enough, not a hard medical ban.

q: Kid line: (2 x age) + 70 until age 10, then 90 like adults. 60 to 100 was the adult pulse range. Which leftover four-year-old systolic cutoff is listed?

opts.t: Double the age and add 70 → 78; below that is hypotension
opts.why: Four-year-old = 8 + 70 = 78.

opts.t: Double the age and add 70 → 90; below that is hypotension
opts.why: 90 is the adult / age-10 number.

opts.t: Use adult 90 for every kid; the equation starts at age ten
opts.why: The equation is for under ten.

opts.t: Use 60 to 100; that was the kid blood-pressure range
opts.why: 60 to 100 was the adult pulse range.

q: Eyes open to sound, confused, localizes pain. 15 is best and 3 is worst. A normal 15 is already off. Which leftover GCS walk is listed?

opts.why: Eyes to sound = 3, confused = 4, localizes = 5 → GCS 12.
That is a normal 15, not this picture.
Sound is 3 not 2. Confused is 4 not 3. Localize is 5 not 4.
Confused (wrong year) is 4. Inappropriate words (purple) would be 3.

q: Year is 1945 versus year is purple. Oriented is answering right. Moans are incomprehensible sounds. Which leftover verbal pair is listed?

opts.t: 1945 is confused (4); purple is inappropriate words (3)
opts.why: Confused = a year, just the wrong year. Inappropriate = not an answer to the question (purple).

opts.t: 1945 is inappropriate (3); purple is confused (4)
opts.why: Those examples are swapped.

opts.t: Both are oriented (5) because they made a sound
opts.why: Oriented is answering the questions right.

opts.t: Both are moans (2) because the year is wrong
opts.why: Moans are not words.

q: Sternal rub. Flexion/decorticate is motor 3. Extension/decerebrate is 2. Obeys is thumbs-up / hold the arm out. Which leftover localizes versus withdraws split is listed?

opts.t: Localize = they know the spot and actively try to stop it; withdraw = passive pull-away
opts.why: Localizes (5): brain knows where; active effort. Withdraws (4): pain somewhere; shrink/turn away.

opts.t: Localize = passive pull-away; withdraw = they know the spot and stop it
opts.why: Those are flipped.

opts.t: Both are decorticate flexion to the core
opts.why: Flexion is motor 3.

opts.t: Both score 6 because any movement is obeys commands
opts.why: Obeys is a requested movement.

q: Light in one should make both constrict. Book Pearl / charted PERRL. Capnography is the medic CO2 tool. Pinpoint is classic opiate; dilated is many stimulants. What named pupil set is that?

opts.t: PERRL / PEARL
opts.why: Conjoined innervation: one light, both constrict. Unequal can be baseline for a few — assume a problem if they cannot tell you.

opts.t: Anisocoria-as-always-normal, with the other pupil left dilated
opts.why: Both should constrict.

opts.t: Cocaine pinpoint and fentanyl dilated
opts.why: Opiates → pinpoint. Stimulants → often dilated.

opts.t: A medic-only capnography adapter check that skips pupils
opts.why: Pupils are a standard vital.

q: Looks like an OD and they are not breathing well. People jump at Narcan. Epi is anaphylaxis. Which leftover test order is true?

opts.t: Open and breathe for them first; Narcan sits after the field impression
opts.why: ABC / oxygen before the condition med (Narcan or Epi). Meds are the bottom of the sheet.

opts.t: Give Narcan first; breathing waits for the reversal to work
opts.why: Do not jump at Narcan and miss open/ventilate.

opts.t: Give the EpiPen first; OD and anaphylaxis share one drug
opts.why: Epi is anaphylaxis. Still after ABCs / oxygen.

opts.t: Skip ABCs; field impression always unlocks meds in the primary
opts.why: Impression and meds come after secondary on the skill sheet.

q: Unstable is almost nonstop. One set of vitals is a snapshot. Pulse back is not breathing back. Which leftover reassess clocks and major-change rule are listed?

opts.t: Critical every 5 minutes; stable every 15; major change, restart primary
opts.why: Unstable q5. Stable q15. Collapse or ROSC: back to LOC / A / B / C. Recheck TQ, splint, pain, BGL, SpO2, restraints until handoff.

opts.t: Critical every 15 minutes; stable every 5; major change, start SAMPLE
opts.why: 5 for critical and 15 for stable. Major change returns to primary, not history.

opts.t: Critical every 5 minutes; skip vitals the second time; one set is a trend
opts.why: Another full set shows trend.

opts.t: Only reassess after hospital handoff; the ride is nap time
opts.why: Do not nap on the ride.

q: Book/NREMT world. Stem already saying you have orders for aspirin is the exception. Real world often offline. Which leftover medication-permission rule is listed?

opts.t: Treat them as online orders; call medical control before you give the drug
opts.why: Call for permission first unless the stem already grants orders. Order: contact, give, reassess.

opts.t: Treat them as offline standing orders; never call on a test
opts.why: The test world reinforces the call first.

opts.t: Give the drug, then call, then reassess — pieces in that order
opts.why: Call before you give.

opts.t: Only glucose needs a phone call; Narcan never does
opts.why: All book meds run as online unless the stem already grants orders.
